newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian mothers ready for captive troop release.
newsitem.headline: Colombian mothers ready for captive troop release.

text.p: Scores of mothers gathered in this remote jungle town on Saturday to await the imminent release of their sons, soldiers taken prisoner by leftist guerrillas nine months ago.

The Catholic Church-led National Conciliation Commission released a video on Saturday showing Red Cross workers registering some of the captive soldiers as heavily-armed guerrillas watched at a secret location in southern Caqueta province -- the final preparations before their handover.
The residents of Cartagena del Chaira spruced up the central plaza to receive the rebel columns expected to pour in just ahead of Sunday's scheduled handover of the prisoners.

The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), Latin America's oldest and largest guerrilla army, has said it will release the 60 soldiers it seized in a battle in neighbouring Putumayo province last August, and 10 marines captured in a firefight in northwest Choco province in January.
"These months have been very hard for me. I've suffered a lot. Nobody is prepared for this situation," one of the mothers, Maria de Silva Tolosa, said.

Conciliation commission member Alvaro Leyva said the 27 soldiers so far registered by the Red Cross were all "happy and very well." The video showed them in their olive green fatigues and clean shaven. All were to be flown by helicopter to another location to join their fellow prisoners. It seemed likely, however, that once assembled the FARC will march them the final few miles (kms) into Cartagena del Chaira or bring them in by river.

The Aug. 30 raid on the Las Delicias base in Putumayo was one of the FARC's greatest military victories in recent years, political analysts said. It also marked the start of Latin America's longest-running hostage crisis -- largely overshadowed by the recent siege of the Japanese Embassy residence in Lima.

Likewise, persuading President Ernesto Samper to temporarily pull the army out of a 5,000 square mile (13,000 sq km) swathe of the province to make way for the prisoners' release is a major political scoop for the FARC, analysts say.

Cartagena del Chaira is a symbolic choice for the troop handover. It is at the heart of a region famed for the production of coca leaf, the raw material for cocaine production. Some observers suggest the Las Delicias attack was timed to coincide with a wave of peasant protests of the government's forced fumigation of illicit coca crops.
The government accuses the FARC of drug trafficking while the rebels argue poor access and infrastructure across the region leaves peasants with no other form of survival except growing coca.

The FARC appeared to have a solid social base in the area. Locals chat with plainclothes rebels patrolling the streets and refer endearingly to the uniformed guerrillas at strategic checkpoints at the approaches to the town as "los 'chachos," or "the lads."
Even some of the mothers who arrived here last week to prepare for the release of their sons have come to see Colombia's three-decade-old Marxist rebel uprising in a different light.

"This experience has helped me see that the conflict we're suffering is the government's fault. The guerrilla is calling for better conditions for the country ... a solution to the problems," Maria Torres said.
